title: How to Build Resilience, Part 1: Acceptance of Reality
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: In the first installment of a resilience series, Dave Stuart Jr. says resilient teachers accept reality, hold a sense of purpose, and adapt. This post treats acceptance. He starts with a plain reminder that teaching is hard, because too much pressure lowers both performance and quality of life. Next he recommends sorting each stressor into what a teacher can and cannot control, with examples such as grading loads, struggling students, and hostile colleagues, and notes that doing so restores a sense of agency. He draws on Viktor Frankl and Admiral Stockdale to argue for pairing hope with a willingness to confront brutal facts. He ends with practical tips, such as responding to setbacks with the phrase of course it did, triaging tasks by their impact on students' long-term flourishing, and acknowledging hard facts while recalling why you teach.
points: Naming that teaching is hard prevents the stress of expecting a job that only feels like love.
Listing what you can and cannot control recovers agency and directs effort to the controllable.
Stockdale's lesson is to hold faith in eventual success alongside realism about the present.
Treating setbacks as expected features of working with people in complex systems makes them easier to respond to calmly.
Triage tasks by impact on students' long-term flourishing and give the closest ones your best hour.
quotes: The hard thing about teaching is that it’s hard. It is, in many moments of the day, work.
You see, too much pressure costs us twice: it lowers our performance — the quality of our work — and it lowers our flourishing — the quality of our lives.
The core competency of this part of resilience is being able to differentiate between what you do have agency over and what you don’t. What can you change, right now today? What can’t you?
When we start sorting work circumstances into buckets of what we can control and what we can’t, an inexplicable joy develops. What is that feeling? It’s a renewed sense of agency.

You see, Stockdale was certain that he would “prevail in the end.” But he says that this certainty alone was deadly. It was the combination of his optimism — “I will prevail” — and his realism — “I am in hell” — that he says made the difference for him.

The goal is to view the things that don’t go according to plan as certainties, not exceptions. They’re facts of our professional life working with humans in complex systems — not weird instances of fate out to crush our dreams.
Every day, that’s the job, and it’s quite doable. It’s almost impossible to not promote the long-term good of young people every day once your mind is set on doing it.
